speaker: Doctor
text: Can you tell me how long you've had these blisters on your forearm and ulcers on your mucosal surfaces? When did you first notice these symptoms?

speaker: Patient
text: 50-year-old female. The patient reports the appearance of blisters on her forearm 3 days ago, accompanied by pain in her left cheek when eating and pain during sexual intercourse for the past week. She has been hiking in the woods recently but denies contact with poison ivy. She has a history of hypertension and osteoarthritis, recently started taking captopril, and discontinued meloxicam 2 weeks ago. Family history includes pernicious anemia and Graves' disease.

speaker: Doctor
text: That timeline of new medications is very concerning; were the blisters triggered shortly after starting captopril, and have you noticed any fever or sensitivity to sunlight? I also need to know if there is any scarring or milia formation in the healed areas, and REQUEST TEST: Complete blood count, Comprehensive metabolic panel, and C3/C4 complement levels.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Based on the biopsy showing acantholysis, desmoglein antibodies, and the clinical presentation of flaccid blisters with mucosal involvement, this is clearly pemphigus vulgaris. The test results definitively rule out cellulitis, which is a bacterial skin infection that does not present with autoantibodies or intraepidermal blistering.

DIAGNOSIS READY: Pemphigus Vulgaris
